notes.definition: The rate of photosynthesis is how quickly a plant makes glucose (or gives out oxygen). It is affected by temperature, light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and the amount of chlorophyll.
explanation: Four factors affect how fast photosynthesis happens: temperature, light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and the amount of chlorophyll. We usually measure the rate by measuring how fast oxygen is produced (for example, counting bubbles from pondweed or collecting the gas in a syringe) or how fast carbon dioxide is used. Rate is calculated as amount of product made ÷ time taken, for example bubbles per minute or cm³ of oxygen per minute.

Light intensity: light transfers the energy needed for photosynthesis. As light intensity increases, the rate increases, because more energy is available. Carbon dioxide concentration: carbon dioxide is a reactant, so increasing its concentration increases the rate. For both factors the graph rises and then levels off, because at some point something else stops the rate rising any further.

Temperature: photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes. As temperature rises, molecules move faster and collide more often, so the rate increases up to an optimum. Above the optimum, enzymes start to denature: the shape of the active site changes, so the rate falls quickly and eventually stops. At low temperatures the rate is slow because enzymes and substrates have little kinetic energy. Amount of chlorophyll: less chlorophyll means less light can be absorbed, so the rate falls. Chlorophyll can be reduced by disease (for example tobacco mosaic virus), a lack of mineral ions or a lack of light.

Required practical 6 investigates the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis. Pondweed is placed in a tube of water with sodium hydrogencarbonate (to supply carbon dioxide), and a lamp is placed at different distances. The number of oxygen bubbles, or the volume of gas collected in a set time, is recorded at each distance. Temperature and carbon dioxide concentration must be kept the same so that only light intensity changes.

Higher tier: the factors interact, and whichever one is in shortest supply is the limiting factor. On a graph, where the line is rising, the factor on the x-axis is limiting. Where the line has levelled off, a different factor is limiting. Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the light source (the inverse square law), so doubling the distance gives one quarter of the light intensity. Growers use this knowledge to decide whether adding heat, light or carbon dioxide to a greenhouse is cost-effective.
keyFacts: Four factors affect the rate: temperature, light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and amount of chlorophyll.
Rate = amount of oxygen produced (or carbon dioxide used) ÷ time.
Increasing light intensity or carbon dioxide concentration increases the rate until another factor stops it rising.
Rate increases with temperature up to an optimum, then falls as enzymes denature.
Less chlorophyll means less light is absorbed, so the rate is lower.
In required practical 6, light intensity is changed by moving the lamp; oxygen bubbles or volume are measured.
Sodium hydrogencarbonate solution supplies carbon dioxide to pondweed.
Higher: the limiting factor is the factor in shortest supply that stops the rate increasing.
Higher: light intensity ∝ 1 ÷ distance², so doubling the distance gives a quarter of the light intensity.

keyTerms.definition: How quickly photosynthesis takes place, often measured as the volume of oxygen produced per unit time.
How bright the light is; the amount of light energy reaching an area each second.
(Higher) The factor in shortest supply that stops the rate of photosynthesis increasing any further.
The temperature at which the rate of an enzyme-controlled process, such as photosynthesis, is fastest.
When an enzyme's active site changes shape (for example at high temperature) so it no longer works.
(Higher) Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the light source.
A chemical added to the water around pondweed to release carbon dioxide so that carbon dioxide is not limiting.

equations.name: Rate of photosynthesis
equations.formula: rate = amount of oxygen produced ÷ time taken
equations.symbols: rate = volume (or number of bubbles) ÷ time

workedExamples.title: Calculating a rate
workedExamples.question: A piece of pondweed produced 6.0 cm³ of oxygen in 4 minutes. Calculate the rate of photosynthesis.
steps: Write the equation: rate = volume of oxygen ÷ time.
Add the unit: cm³ per minute.

workedExamples.title: Using the inverse square law (Higher)
workedExamples.question: A lamp is moved from 10 cm to 30 cm away from a plant. By what factor does the light intensity change?
steps: The distance has increased by a factor of 30 ÷ 10 = 3.
So the light intensity changes by a factor of 1 ÷ 3² = 1 ÷ 9.
workedExamples.answer: The light intensity becomes 1/9 of its original value (about 0.11 times).

workedExamples.title: Calculating relative light intensity (Higher)
workedExamples.question: Relative light intensity can be calculated as 10 000 ÷ d², where d is in cm. Calculate the relative light intensity when the lamp is 20 cm from the pondweed.
steps: This is in arbitrary units because it is only used to compare distances.

workedExamples.title: Calculating a mean and excluding an anomaly
workedExamples.question: A student counted bubbles per minute at one distance: 18, 20, 31, 19. Calculate the mean rate.
steps: Spot the anomaly: 31 is far from the other values, so leave it out.
Divide by the number of values used: 57 ÷ 3 = 19.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that increasing light intensity always increases the rate of photosynthesis.
misconceptions.right: In fact the rate only increases until another factor, such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, becomes limiting. Then the graph levels off.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think enzymes are 'killed' at high temperatures.
misconceptions.right: In fact enzymes are proteins, not living things. High temperatures denature them: the active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think moving a lamp twice as far away halves the light intensity.
misconceptions.right: In fact (Higher) light intensity follows the inverse square law, so doubling the distance reduces it to one quarter.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think low temperatures denature enzymes.
misconceptions.right: In fact at low temperatures enzymes simply work slowly because molecules have less kinetic energy. They are not denatured and work again when warmed.

realWorld: Commercial greenhouses use paraffin heaters, which warm the air and release carbon dioxide, plus artificial lighting, to increase the rate of photosynthesis and grow crops faster and out of season.
Growers use data on limiting factors to decide whether paying for extra heating, lighting or carbon dioxide will increase yield enough to make a profit.
Vertical farms grow salad crops indoors under LED lights, controlling light intensity, temperature and carbon dioxide so none of them limits growth.
higherTier: The factors interact, and any one of them may be the limiting factor: the factor in shortest supply that stops the rate increasing.

Interpreting graphs with two or three factors: where a line rises, the factor on the x-axis is limiting; where it is flat, another factor is limiting. A higher plateau when carbon dioxide or temperature is raised shows that factor was limiting.
Inverse proportion: light intensity ∝ 1 ÷ distance² (the inverse square law). Doubling the distance gives one quarter of the light intensity; halving it gives four times the light intensity.

Using data to relate limiting factors to the cost-effectiveness of adding heat, light or carbon dioxide to greenhouses: extra inputs are only worthwhile if the increase in yield is worth more than the cost, and only if that factor is actually limiting.
examTips: When explaining a graph that levels off, name the limiting factor in each part: 'light intensity is limiting on the rising section; carbon dioxide concentration or temperature is limiting on the flat section'.
For high temperatures, write 'enzymes are denatured' and mention the active site changing shape. Never say enzymes are killed.
In the required practical, the control variables are usually temperature and carbon dioxide concentration (and the same pondweed). A beaker of water or an LED bulb reduces heating from the lamp.
For inverse square law questions, square the distance ratio and then flip it. Show this step clearly to earn the method mark.
When asked about greenhouse costs, compare the extra income from the increased yield with the cost of the heat, light or carbon dioxide, using numbers from the data.
summary: Rate is affected by temperature, light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and amount of chlorophyll.
Rate = amount of oxygen produced ÷ time.
Light and carbon dioxide graphs rise then level off; temperature graphs rise to an optimum then fall sharply.
Required practical 6: vary lamp distance, count bubbles or measure gas volume, keep temperature and carbon dioxide constant.
Higher: the limiting factor is the one in shortest supply.
Higher: greenhouse inputs are worthwhile only if the extra yield pays for them.

flashcards.front: Four factors that affect the rate of photosynthesis
flashcards.back: Temperature, light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration, amount of chlorophyll.

flashcards.front: How do you calculate the rate of photosynthesis?
flashcards.back: Amount of oxygen produced (or bubbles) ÷ time.

flashcards.front: Why does rate fall above the optimum temperature?
flashcards.back: The enzymes controlling photosynthesis denature; their active sites change shape.

flashcards.front: Why does less chlorophyll reduce the rate?
flashcards.back: Less light energy can be absorbed.
Light intensity (changed by moving the lamp to different distances).
Rate of photosynthesis: number of oxygen bubbles or volume of oxygen per minute.

flashcards.front: Why add sodium hydrogencarbonate to the water?
flashcards.back: It releases carbon dioxide so carbon dioxide does not limit the rate.

flashcards.front: How can you stop the lamp heating the pondweed?
flashcards.back: Use an LED bulb or place a beaker of water between the lamp and the tube; monitor with a thermometer.
The factor in shortest supply that stops the rate of photosynthesis increasing.

flashcards.front: On a rate against light intensity graph, what is limiting on the flat part? (Higher)
flashcards.back: Not light: another factor such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature.
Light intensity ∝ 1 ÷ distance². Double the distance gives 1/4 of the intensity.

flashcards.front: If the lamp distance is halved, what happens to light intensity? (Higher)
When is adding carbon dioxide to a greenhouse cost-effective? (Higher)
flashcards.back: When carbon dioxide is the limiting factor and the extra yield is worth more than the cost.

questions.question: Which of these affects the rate of photosynthesis?
options: Concentration of oxygen in the air
Amount of chlorophyll
Concentration of nitrogen in the air
Colour of the plant pot
markScheme: 1 mark: amount of chlorophyll
questions.explanation: The four factors you need to know are temperature, light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and amount of chlorophyll. Oxygen is a product, and nitrogen gas is not used in photosynthesis.

questions.question: Why does the rate of photosynthesis fall quickly at temperatures well above the optimum?
options: The plant runs out of light
Carbon dioxide cannot dissolve
The plant cells start to respire
The enzymes controlling photosynthesis are denatured
markScheme: 1 mark: the enzymes controlling photosynthesis are denatured
questions.explanation: High temperatures change the shape of enzyme active sites so they no longer work. Plant cells respire all the time, not just when hot, and the amount of light does not depend on temperature.

A student investigated the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis.

options: The number of bubbles produced
The distance of the lamp (light intensity)
The temperature of the water
The type of pondweed
markScheme: 1 mark: the distance of the lamp (light intensity)
questions.explanation: The independent variable is the one you change on purpose: the lamp distance, which changes light intensity. The number of bubbles is the dependent variable. Temperature and type of pondweed are control variables.

questions.question: Why should a student use an LED lamp rather than a filament lamp when investigating the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis?
options: LED lamps produce less heat, so temperature stays more constant
LED lamps produce carbon dioxide
LED lamps give out light only at one distance
LED lamps make the pondweed produce more chlorophyll
markScheme: 1 mark: LED lamps produce less heat, so the temperature stays more constant
questions.explanation: Temperature is a control variable. A hot filament lamp moved close to the pondweed would warm the water and change the rate, making the test unfair. LEDs transfer far less energy by heating.

questions.question: Why is sodium hydrogencarbonate added to the water around the pondweed in an investigation into the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis?
options: To kill bacteria in the water
To keep the temperature constant
To provide carbon dioxide so it does not limit the rate
To provide oxygen for the pondweed
markScheme: 1 mark: to provide carbon dioxide so it does not limit the rate
questions.explanation: Sodium hydrogencarbonate releases carbon dioxide into the water. This makes sure the pondweed has plenty of carbon dioxide, so light intensity is the factor being tested. It does not control temperature or supply oxygen.

Amount of oxygen
Carbon dioxide concentration
Amount of water
markScheme: 1 mark: carbon dioxide concentration
questions.explanation: Raising carbon dioxide raised the plateau, so carbon dioxide must have been limiting there. Light intensity cannot be limiting on the flat part, because increasing it had no effect.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a limiting factor?
options: The factor that is in largest supply
The factor in shortest supply that stops the rate increasing
Any factor that makes the rate of photosynthesis zero
The factor that a scientist chooses to change
markScheme: 1 mark: the factor in shortest supply that stops the rate increasing
questions.explanation: A limiting factor holds back the rate because it is in short supply; increasing it would increase the rate. The factor a scientist changes is the independent variable, which is a different idea.

questions.question: A plant has a disease that turns patches of its leaves yellow because they have less chlorophyll. What happens to its rate of photosynthesis?
options: It decreases because less light is absorbed
It increases because more light reaches the leaf
It stays the same because chlorophyll is not needed
It increases because yellow leaves are warmer
markScheme: 1 mark: it decreases because less light is absorbed
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy for photosynthesis. Less chlorophyll means less light is absorbed, so less glucose is made.

questions.question: A lamp is moved from 40 cm to 20 cm away from a plant. What happens to the light intensity reaching the plant?
options: It halves
It doubles
It becomes 4 times greater
It becomes one quarter
markScheme: 1 mark: it becomes 4 times greater
questions.explanation: Light intensity ∝ 1 ÷ d². The distance is halved, so intensity is multiplied by 1 ÷ (0.5)² = 4. 'It doubles' is the common mistake made by forgetting to square.

questions.question: Why is the rate of photosynthesis slow at 5 °C?
options: The enzymes are denatured
There is no light at low temperatures
The stomata are permanently closed
Molecules have little kinetic energy, so enzyme-controlled reactions are slow
markScheme: 1 mark: molecules have little kinetic energy, so enzyme-controlled reactions are slow
questions.explanation: At low temperature, enzyme and substrate molecules move slowly and collide less often. Enzymes are not denatured by cold; they work again when warmed. Light does not depend on temperature.

questions.question: On a dull winter day, a grower adds extra carbon dioxide to a well-heated greenhouse, but the rate of photosynthesis hardly changes. What is the most likely reason?
options: Carbon dioxide is toxic to plants
Light intensity is the limiting factor
The plants have too much chlorophyll
Temperature is too high
markScheme: 1 mark: light intensity is the limiting factor
questions.explanation: On a dull day light is in short supply, so adding carbon dioxide cannot raise the rate. The greenhouse is heated, so temperature is not the problem. Extra carbon dioxide would be wasted money.

questions.question:
A student counted the bubbles of oxygen given off by some pondweed.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the mean rate of photosynthesis in bubbles per minute over the 3 minutes.
markScheme: 1 mark: total bubbles = 36 and 36 ÷ 3
1 mark: 12 bubbles/min
questions.explanation: Total bubbles = 11 + 13 + 12 = 36. Rate = number of bubbles ÷ time = 36 ÷ 3 = 12 bubbles per minute. Multiplying instead of dividing (108) is a common slip.

questions.question:
A student used a gas syringe to collect the oxygen given off by some pondweed.
Figure 1 shows the results.
Use Figure 1 to calculate the rate of oxygen production over the first 5 minutes.
Give your answer in cm³ per minute.

markScheme: 1 mark: volume at 5 minutes read as 4.8 cm³ and 4.8 ÷ 5
1 mark: 0.96 cm³/min
questions.explanation: From Figure 1, the volume at 5 minutes is 4.8 cm³. Rate = volume ÷ time = 4.8 ÷ 5 = 0.96 cm³/min. Collecting gas in a syringe is more accurate than counting bubbles because bubbles vary in size.

questions.question:
Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the light source.
A lamp is moved from 10 cm to 20 cm away from some pondweed.
Calculate the new light intensity as a fraction of the original light intensity.
Give your answer as a decimal.
markScheme: 1 mark: intensity ∝ 1 ÷ d², distance doubled so factor = 1 ÷ 2²
1 mark: 0.25 (one quarter)
questions.explanation: Doubling the distance means intensity is multiplied by 1 ÷ 2² = 1 ÷ 4 = 0.25. Answering 0.5 ignores the square in the inverse square law.

questions.question:
Use the equation:
relative light intensity = 10 000 ÷ d²
where d is the distance of the lamp from the plant in cm.
Calculate the relative light intensity when the lamp is 25 cm from the plant.
questions.explanation: Square the distance first (25² = 625), then divide: 10 000 ÷ 625 = 16. Dividing by 25 without squaring gives 400, which is wrong.

questions.question:
A student counted the oxygen bubbles given off per minute by pondweed at the same light intensity.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the mean number of bubbles per minute.
Do not include the anomalous result in your calculation.
markScheme: 1 mark: identifies 35 as anomalous and uses (22 + 24 + 23) ÷ 3
1 mark: 23 bubbles/min
questions.explanation: 35 is much higher than the others, so it is anomalous. (22 + 24 + 23) ÷ 3 = 69 ÷ 3 = 23. Including 35 gives 26, which is not a fair mean.

questions.question:
Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the light source.
At 20 cm from a lamp, the light intensity reaching a leaf is 50 arbitrary units.
Calculate the light intensity when the lamp is moved to 10 cm from the leaf.
markScheme: 1 mark: distance halved so intensity × 2² (= × 4)
1 mark: 200 arbitrary units
questions.explanation: Light intensity ∝ 1 ÷ d². Halving the distance multiplies intensity by 4, so 50 × 4 = 200 au. Just doubling to 100 forgets to square.

questions.question:
A student measured the rate of photosynthesis of a plant at two carbon dioxide concentrations.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the percentage increase in the rate of photosynthesis.

headers: Rate of photosynthesis in bubbles per minute

markScheme: 1 mark: 75%
questions.explanation: Percentage change = (new − original) ÷ original × 100 = 6 ÷ 8 × 100 = 75%. Dividing by 14 instead of the original value gives 42.9%, which is wrong.

questions.question: Name two factors, other than light intensity, that affect the rate of photosynthesis.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two from: temperature; carbon dioxide concentration; amount of chlorophyll
questions.explanation: The four factors in the specification are temperature, light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and amount of chlorophyll. Water is a reactant, but it is rarely limiting and is not one of the four factors you need.

questions.question: Explain why the rate of photosynthesis increases as light intensity increases.
markScheme: 1 mark: light transfers the energy needed for photosynthesis
1 mark: more light means more energy is absorbed by chlorophyll, so more glucose / oxygen is made per minute
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis is endothermic, so it needs energy from light. Brighter light means more energy is available each second, so the reaction goes faster until another factor becomes limiting.

questions.question:
A student investigated the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis in pondweed.
Give two variables the student should control.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two from: temperature of the water; carbon dioxide (sodium hydrogencarbonate) concentration; same type / length / piece of pondweed; same time period for counting
questions.explanation: Temperature and carbon dioxide concentration also affect the rate, so they must be kept the same. Otherwise you could not tell whether a change in rate was caused by light intensity.

questions.question: Counting bubbles is not an accurate way to measure the rate of photosynthesis. Give one reason why, and suggest a better method.
markScheme: 1 mark: bubbles are different sizes / bubbles may be released too fast to count
1 mark: collect the gas and measure its volume, e.g. with a gas syringe or upturned measuring cylinder
questions.explanation: Each bubble may contain a different volume of gas. Measuring the total volume of gas collected in a set time gives a more accurate measure of oxygen produced.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows the rate of photosynthesis at different light intensities at two carbon dioxide concentrations. The temperature was kept the same.
Explain the results shown in Figure 1.
acceptedAnswers: light is limiting at low light intensity
carbon dioxide is limiting at high light intensity
more carbon dioxide raises the plateau
markScheme: 1 mark: at low light intensity, light is the limiting factor, so extra carbon dioxide has no effect / lines are the same
1 mark: at high light intensity, carbon dioxide becomes the limiting factor (for 0.04%)
1 mark: with more carbon dioxide (0.10%), more can be used, so the rate rises higher before levelling off
questions.explanation: Only the factor in shortest supply affects the rate. When light is very low, extra carbon dioxide makes no difference. Once light is plentiful, carbon dioxide limits the rate, so the higher concentration gives a higher plateau.

questions.question: Describe and explain the effect of temperature on the rate of photosynthesis above the optimum temperature.
markScheme: 1 mark: the rate decreases (quickly)
1 mark: because enzymes are denatured / active site changes shape so substrate no longer fits
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis is enzyme-controlled. Above the optimum, bonds holding the enzyme's shape break, the active site changes shape and fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form.

questions.question:
A tomato grower can add heating and extra carbon dioxide to a greenhouse.
Table 1 shows the grower's weekly data. Tomatoes sell for £2 per kg.
Evaluate whether the grower should add heating, and whether they should also add carbon dioxide.
Use data from Table 1 in your answer.

headers: Mass of tomatoes in kg per week
rows: With heating and extra carbon dioxide

markScheme: 1 mark: heating gives 8 kg extra = £16, which is more than £10, so heating is worth adding (£6 profit)
1 mark: carbon dioxide gives a further 12 kg = £24, which is less than its extra £30 cost (£40 − £10) (£6 loss)
1 mark: conclusion: add heating but not carbon dioxide (at these prices)
questions.explanation: Extra inputs are only cost-effective if the value of the extra crop is greater than the cost. Heating increases income by £16 for £10. Carbon dioxide increases income by £24 but costs £30, so it reduces profit.

questions.question: In an investigation into the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis in pondweed, state what is measured to find the rate of photosynthesis.
markScheme: 1 mark: the number of oxygen bubbles (or volume of oxygen/gas) produced in a set time
questions.explanation: Oxygen is a product, so the faster it is produced, the faster photosynthesis is happening. It must be measured over a fixed time to give a rate.

questions.question: Tobacco mosaic virus causes a mosaic pattern of pale patches on leaves where chlorophyll is lost. Explain why infected plants grow more slowly.
markScheme: 1 mark: less chlorophyll so less light is absorbed / less photosynthesis
1 mark: so less glucose is made for growth
questions.explanation: Less chlorophyll reduces the rate of photosynthesis, so less glucose is available to make new cells (such as cellulose and proteins), and growth is stunted.

questions.question: Describe a method to investigate how light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis in pondweed. Include how you would make your results valid.
markScheme: Indicative content: place pondweed in a boiling tube of water with sodium hydrogencarbonate (excess carbon dioxide); place a lamp a set distance away, e.g. 10 cm, measured with a metre rule; leave for a few minutes to acclimatise; count bubbles (or collect gas in a gas syringe / measuring cylinder) for a set time, e.g. 1 minute; repeat at different distances, e.g. 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 cm; repeat each distance three times and calculate a mean; control temperature using an LED bulb or a beaker of water as a heat shield and check with a thermometer; keep carbon dioxide concentration and pondweed the same; work in a darkened room so the lamp is the only light source; calculate rate = bubbles ÷ time and plot rate against distance or light intensity.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a clear, logical method that could be followed to get valid results, including the independent variable, how rate is measured, timing, repeats and control of temperature and carbon dioxide.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a method with most of the main steps but some gaps, e.g. control variables or repeats missing.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some relevant steps but not in a logical order, or the method would not give valid results.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The method must change only light intensity (distance), measure oxygen production over a fixed time, repeat for reliability, and control temperature and carbon dioxide. Mentioning the darkened room and heat shield shows you understand validity.

questions.question:
A scientist measured the rate of photosynthesis at different light intensities under three conditions.
Figure 1 shows the results.
Line A: 0.04% carbon dioxide at 20 °C
Line B: 0.10% carbon dioxide at 20 °C
Line C: 0.10% carbon dioxide at 30 °C
Explain what these results show about limiting factors.
markScheme: Indicative content: at low light intensity all lines are the same, so light is the limiting factor; for line A, the plateau is caused by carbon dioxide being limiting, shown because B (more CO₂) levels off higher; for line B, the plateau is caused by temperature being limiting, shown because C (higher temperature) levels off higher; any one of the factors can be limiting; the factor in shortest supply limits the rate; to get the highest rate all factors must be increased together.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correctly identifies the limiting factor for each line at high light intensity, uses comparisons between lines as evidence, and states light is limiting at low intensity.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): identifies at least one limiting factor correctly or describes the trends with limited explanation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Compare pairs of lines that differ in only one factor. A and B differ only in carbon dioxide, so CO₂ limited A. B and C differ only in temperature, so temperature limited B. At low light, light is limiting for all three.
